drapeaux.note: Langue d'origine : anglais ; auteur : Luke Howard (Essay on the Modification of Clouds). Retraduit depuis le français, à remplacer par le texte original.

titre: The chemist who gave clouds their names
accroche: In December 1802, a chemist with a hobby in meteorology invents, for a London learned society, the Latin words that still designate clouds.
contenu_vulgarise:
In December 1802, in a room in London, a small audience listens to a talk that no professional meteorologist has asked for. The speaker, Luke Howard, is thirty years old. He makes and sells chemicals for a living; watching the sky is his pastime. Before the Askesian Society, a circle of curious minds that meets to discuss natural science, he presents a paper with a modest title: “On the Modification of Clouds.” In it he proposes what no one has done before: giving clouds fixed names, in Latin, as is done for plants and animals.

## A vocabulary designed for forms that never stop changing

Howard openly takes his inspiration from Carl von Linné, the Swedish naturalist whose classification of species had brought order to natural history some fifty years earlier. But a cloud is not a plant: it never stays identical to itself. The real problem Howard has to solve is therefore how to name transformations.

His solution comes down to three basic words, chosen for their literal meaning. Cirrus, the lock of hair or filament, for thin, fibrous high-altitude clouds. Cumulus, the heap, for clouds that pile up in relief. Stratus, the layer, for clouds that spread out flat. To these three forms, Howard adds combinations: cirro-cumulus, cirro-stratus, cumulo-stratus, and a fourth category, nimbus, for the cloud that has ceased to be a form and has started to rain. The system does not freeze a snapshot of the sky: it describes one cloud in the process of becoming another cloud, with a word for each stage.

## An amateur, remembered for two centuries

Howard's paper appears in 1803 in the Philosophical Magazine, then in book form. It circulates quickly outside England: a German translation of 1815 catches the eye of Goethe, who devotes verses of gratitude to him for having, he writes, fixed the limit of what had remained vague and given it a fitting name.

No scientific authority imposes this vocabulary at the time. It takes hold on its own, through use, for nearly a century, before an international meteorological congress adopts it to build the first International Cloud Atlas, in 1896. The World Meteorological Organization, which publishes the International Cloud Atlas today, has refined the nomenclature, added species and varieties, but has never replaced the four Latin roots of 1802.

The vocabulary that a thirty-year-old chemist invents in a single evening, to entertain a private club, is still the official way of describing the sky, in weather bulletins, textbooks, and WMO reports, more than two centuries later.

quiz.question: Why has Luke Howard's classification endured, even though clouds constantly change shape?
choix: Because it provides for compound forms, able to describe one cloud turning into another
Because an international treaty fixed its definition as early as 1802
Because each Latin name corresponds to a fixed, measurable altitude
Because the World Meteorological Organization forbids adding new terms to it
quiz.explication: Howard did not just name states but provided for intermediate forms (cirro-cumulus, cumulo-stratus...): the system describes a transformation, not a snapshot. Nothing was fixed by treaty in 1802. Adoption came through use, then through an international congress nearly a century later, and the WMO has since added species and varieties without touching the four Latin roots.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was Luke Howard's profession when he presented his paper in December 1802?
choix: A manufacturer and seller of chemicals, a meteorologist only as an amateur
A professor of meteorology at the University of London
An Anglican clergyman passionate about astronomy
A cartographer employed by the British Royal Navy
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that Howard makes and sells chemicals for a living, and that watching the sky is only a pastime for him at the time of his talk.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which naturalist does Luke Howard openly take as his inspiration in building his system of Latin names?
choix: Charles Darwin, for his theory of natural selection
Carl von Linné, for his classification of animal and plant species
Georges Cuvier, for his work in comparative anatomy
Alexander von Humboldt, for his maps of world vegetation
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Howard openly takes his inspiration from Carl von Linné, whose classification of species had brought order to natural history some fifty years earlier.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the term nimbus denote in Luke Howard's system?
choix: A thin, fibrous high-altitude cloud, like a lock of hair
A cloud that spreads out flat and covers the sky uniformly
A cloud that has ceased to be a form and has started to rain
A cloud that builds up in relief like a stacked heap
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Howard adds a fourth category, nimbus, to designate the cloud that has ceased to be an identifiable form and has started to rain, distinct from the three basic forms.
